strategy: The solver first checks for infeasibility. It reports "infeasible" for an unknown job or resource, a demand above capacity, or a precedence cycle (found with Kahn's topological sort). Otherwise it computes a lower bound from the critical path (with release times) and per-resource energy, and stops early whenever a schedule reaches that bound. Schedules come from a serial schedule-generation scheme over precedence-feasible activity lists. Each one is improved by forward-backward justification, and the improved start order is written back into the list. The search seeds with 9 classic priority rules (LST, LFT, longest tail, earliest start, successor count, GRPW, work, release) plus random biased sampling. It then runs a time-bounded activity-list genetic algorithm with precedence-preserving two-point crossover and insertion mutation. A final verifier checks the best schedule; if it ever fails, the solver falls back to a trivially valid one-job-at-a-time sequence. No LLM is used.

The solver first checks feasibility. It returns "infeasible" if any job references an unknown job or resource, needs more units than a resource's capacity, or if Kahn's algorithm finds a precedence cycle. For feasible instances it builds an active schedule with a Serial Schedule Generation Scheme. Each job is placed at the earliest time that satisfies its release, its predecessors and the per-time resource profiles. The scheme is seeded with several classic priority rules: longest tail / critical path, latest start, most successors and earliest head. These are refined by forward-backward improvement (justification), and the best lists are then improved by randomized activity-list local search (precedence-respecting insertion moves, accepting equal moves) with periodic justification and restarts. Everything runs in a single code node under a ~1.1 s budget, with an early stop if the makespan reaches the lower bound (the larger of the critical path and the resource-energy bounds).

Validation runs first. It checks for unknown job or resource references, for any requirement larger than its resource's capacity, and for precedence cycles using Kahn's topological sort. If none of these is found, the instance is reported feasible. A serial schedule-generation scheme turns any precedence-consistent job order into a feasible schedule. It places each job at its earliest start that respects release time, predecessors and capacity, jumping past the last conflicting slot. Every order is then improved by forward–backward justification: the schedule is right-justified, ignoring releases, and the resulting order is left-justified again. Several priority rules seed the search: longest tail, latest finish time, slack, earliest start, successor count and resource-weighted tail. After that, the time budget goes to regret-biased random sampling and an insertion-move local search with restarts, stopping early if the schedule reaches a computed lower bound. A final validator checks the result. If it ever fails, a trivially valid sequential schedule is returned instead.

The solution runs as one deterministic code node; an LLM call would add nothing here. It first checks the instance and answers "infeasible" for unknown job or resource references, demands above capacity, or a precedence cycle (found with Kahn's topological sort). It then computes critical-path heads and tails, a lower bound (critical path plus per-resource energy bounds), and latest finish times. It builds schedules with a Serial Schedule Generation Scheme from several priority rules and improves each with forward-backward justification (right-justify by decreasing finish time, then left-justify by start order) until it stops improving. Until about 0.9 s have passed or the lower bound is reached, it keeps sampling randomly perturbed priority keys and repeats the improvement. The best schedule is checked against all hard constraints before output, with a safe one-job-at-a-time schedule as a fallback.

The solution is one deterministic code node, with no LLM call. It first checks feasibility: an unknown predecessor or resource, more units than a resource's capacity, or a precedence cycle (found with Kahn's topological sort) returns "infeasible". Otherwise it computes a lower bound from release-aware critical paths and per-resource energy bounds, and stops early if it reaches that bound. It builds schedules with a serial schedule-generation scheme that respects releases, precedences and integer-time capacity profiles. It seeds the search with eight priority rules (latest start time, tail length, earliest start, successor count, energy-weighted variants and others), each refined by forward-backward justification passes. It then spends the remaining time budget (about 0.9 s total) on biased random sampling of noisy priority keys and on a precedence-preserving shift local search with restarts; the result is always rebuilt by the forward scheme, so every "ok" answer satisfies the constraints.

The solver first validates the instance. It answers infeasible if a job names an unknown job or resource, needs more units than a resource's capacity, or if Kahn's topological sort finds a precedence cycle. For valid instances it computes a lower bound from release-aware heads/tails and per-resource energy, so it can stop early once a schedule reaches that bound. Schedules are built by an integer-time serial schedule-generation scheme that decodes priority keys (lowest key among precedence-eligible jobs goes first). Each decoded schedule is improved by forward-backward justification: shift every job as late as possible, then re-pack everything as early as possible, and repeat while the makespan drops. A time-budgeted search runs until about 0.95 s or the bound is reached: it tries seven priority rules (LST, LFT, tail, head, successor count, work), then random sampling around LST and perturbations of the best and elite key vectors.

First the instance is checked for infeasibility: an unknown job or resource, a job needing more units than a resource's capacity, or a precedence cycle (found by topological sort). If it is feasible, a serial schedule generator places jobs in a precedence-respecting order. Each job goes at the earliest integer time that respects its release time, its predecessors and the per-time resource usage. Starting orders come from several priority rules (latest finish, latest start, earliest start, longest tail, most successors, resource work). Each is improved by forward-backward justification passes. The rest of the time budget (0.85 s) goes to biased random sampling plus local search that moves jobs within their precedence window, with restarts from the best schedule. The search stops early when the makespan reaches a lower bound (critical path with releases, or a per-resource energy bound).
This uses no LLM; it validates the instance, then searches for a good schedule within a fixed time budget.

A single deterministic code node handles everything, with no LLM call. It first validates the instance: unknown job or resource references, units above capacity, and precedence cycles (found by Kahn's topological sort) each produce "infeasible". Otherwise it computes a lower bound from the critical path (heads/tails) and per-resource energy bounds above each release value. It builds a time-indexed serial schedule-generation scheme over precedence-feasible activity lists. These lists are seeded from several priority rules: longest tail, earliest head, slack, work-weighted tail and number of successors. Each decoded schedule is improved by forward-backward justification: right-justify in place, then re-decode in start-time order. A local search runs until the bound is reached or about 0.85 s has passed. It mutates the activity list with precedence-respecting insertion moves, accepts equal or better schedules, and occasionally restarts from the best list or a noisy priority list. A final checker validates the schedule and falls back to a trivially valid sequential schedule if it fails.

The solver first validates the instance. It reports "infeasible" for unknown job references, unknown resources, demand above capacity, or a precedence cycle (found with Kahn's topological sort). For feasible instances it builds schedules with a Serial Schedule Generation Scheme (SSGS) on a time-indexed resource profile. Starting lists come from several priority rules (longest tail path, release/head, successor count, resource work) plus biased-random sampling. Every promising schedule is improved by forward-backward double justification, which never makes the makespan worse and respects release times. The remaining time budget, about 1.1 s, goes to local search over precedence-feasible activity lists, using random insertion moves, plateau acceptance and restarts. The search stops early when it reaches a computed lower bound (critical path with releases, plus a per-resource energy bound). Before output, the final schedule is checked against every hard constraint, with a guaranteed-valid sequential schedule as fallback.

The pipeline is pure code with no LLM calls, because the problem is a small exact combinatorial search where a model adds latency but no value. It first validates the instance. It returns "infeasible" for an unknown predecessor, an unknown resource, a demand above capacity, or a precedence cycle (Kahn's algorithm). Otherwise it builds schedules with the serial schedule-generation scheme over time-indexed resource profiles. It seeds this with several deterministic priority rules (critical-path tail, total successors, release, resource load), then runs randomized biased-key sampling. Every schedule is refined by forward-backward improvement until the makespan stops dropping. Search stops early if it reaches a computed lower bound (critical path with releases, or resource energy), and in any case after about 1.1 s.

The solution is a single deterministic code node and makes no LLM calls. It first checks the input for unknown job or resource references, demands above capacity, and precedence cycles (using Kahn's algorithm), and returns "infeasible" if any are found. Otherwise it computes a lower bound from the critical path with release times and from per-resource work, so it can stop early once the bound is reached. Schedules come from a serial schedule-generation scheme that places each job at the earliest time where precedence and capacity allow, using jump-ahead conflict scanning. Job orders are drawn by biased random sampling over several priority rules (longest tail, earliest start, most successors, resource-weighted tail), and good schedules are improved by in-place forward-backward double justification. For the rest of a roughly 0.95 s budget, a local search applies precedence-safe insertion moves to activity lists from an elite pool, with restarts. The final answer is checked against every hard constraint, with a fully serial schedule as a fallback that is always valid.

A single deterministic code node first checks feasibility. It returns "infeasible" when a job references an unknown job or resource, when a job needs more units than a resource's capacity, or when Kahn's topological sort finds a precedence cycle. Otherwise it builds schedules with a serial schedule-generation scheme over a time-indexed resource profile; this always gives a valid schedule that respects release times and precedences. The candidate orders come from several priority rules: longest tail (LST), earliest start, most total successors, rank-weighted positional weight, and longest duration. Biased random sampling adds more. Each candidate is improved by forward-backward justification: right-justify against the current makespan, then re-run the forward pass using the order of the justified start times. A genetic algorithm then runs until about 0.9 s. It uses one-point crossover and precedence-safe mutations on activity lists and keeps improved lists back in the population. It stops early if the makespan reaches a critical-path or energy lower bound. A final validator checks the best schedule and falls back to a sequential schedule if anything fails.

A validation node first checks for unknown job or resource references, demands that exceed a resource's capacity, and precedence cycles (using Kahn's algorithm). If it finds any, it returns "infeasible" with a reason. Feasible instances go to a solver that builds schedules with a serial schedule-generation scheme. Jobs are taken from a priority heap once all their predecessors are placed, and each is put at the earliest time that respects its release, its predecessors and resource capacity. Each schedule is improved by forward-backward passes, which reschedule backward from the finish times and then forward again. The search starts from several priority rules (longest tail, head minus tail, earliest head, most successors, largest resource load). It then runs a randomized multi-start and perturbs the best schedule's start-order keys within a 0.9 s budget. It stops early if it reaches a computed lower bound (critical path with releases, resource energy, and a set of jobs that cannot overlap). On 30 random local test instances every schedule passed an independent checker, and makespans averaged about 0.97 of my own lower bound.

A single code node first validates the instance. It returns "infeasible" if a job references an unknown predecessor or resource, if a job needs more units than a resource's capacity, or if Kahn's topological sort finds a precedence cycle. For a feasible instance it builds schedules with a serial schedule-generation scheme: jobs are taken in precedence-feasible order by a priority key and each is placed at its earliest start that respects release times, predecessors and resource capacity. Every schedule is then improved by forward-backward improvement: the schedule is mirrored and packed backward, then repacked forward using the backward start times as priorities, repeated while it helps. The search starts from classic priority rules and then, within about one second, alternates noisy rules with random perturbations of the best schedule's start times. It stops early when the makespan equals a computed lower bound (critical path with release times, or a per-resource energy bound).

A deterministic code node first checks feasibility: unknown job or resource references, demand above capacity, and precedence cycles found with Kahn's algorithm. For feasible instances, priority-rule serial SGS with forward-backward justification and a GA with an activity-list encoding produce a strong incumbent within about 0.55 s. A depth-first branch-and-bound over canonical serial-SGS orders then uses the remaining budget, up to about 1.1 s in total. Canonical orders are those whose (start, rank) pairs strictly increase, which avoids duplicate schedules. Nodes are pruned with dynamic critical-path and profile-energy bounds against the incumbent. A final validator checks the best schedule and falls back to a sequential schedule if anything fails.
change:
DIAGNOSIS: The program only searches by sampling. The GA and the forward-backward improvement explore activity lists at random and never check the space of active schedules systematically. On small and medium instances it often stops at a local optimum while better orders still exist, and it cannot tell when it has already reached the optimum. In families with tight, nearly exclusive resources or late release times, the remaining time goes to a GA that has stagnated instead of a directed search. A second, separate effect is that the hidden lower bound is weak on some instances. For example, the zero_durations case at makespan 26 already appears optimal, so part of the gap is not recoverable. After a shorter GA warm start, a time-bounded depth-first branch-and-bound runs over serial-SGS orders, with the GA result as the incumbent. It branches only on canonical orders, meaning the (start, topological rank) pairs must strictly increase. Every active schedule is produced by the serial SGS on its own start-sorted list, so this enumerates each active schedule exactly once, and the optimum is among them. The search is still complete, but with far fewer duplicate schedules. Each node is pruned by two bounds:
- **Dynamic critical path:** every unscheduled job must start at or after the last start time, and its predecessors' finish times push it later.
- **Resource energy:** the remaining work on each resource must fit into the free capacity of the current profile before the incumbent's makespan.

strategy: A single code node first checks feasibility: unknown job or resource references, demand above capacity, and precedence cycles found with Kahn's algorithm. For feasible instances, priority rules plus biased sampling build a population of activity lists. Each list is decoded by serial SGS and improved by forward-backward justification. GA phase 1 then evolves the population, with an insertion local search on the incumbent. Next, X's canonical-order branch-and-bound with critical-path and energy pruning tries to beat or prove the GA incumbent. If it does not prove optimality, its result is put back into the population for GA phase 2. All phases stop when the strengthened lower bound is reached, and a validator with a sequential fallback guarantees a valid answer.
change: X and Y share the same heuristic core and score the same on dev (0.927). So within the time limit, X's branch-and-bound (B&B) never found a better schedule than Y's longer GA. Several of the weakest instances are already optimal. For example, the zero_durations case at makespan 26 cannot go lower: the oven-4 job J4 cannot overlap the J5→J2 chain after time 10. The remaining gap comes from the hidden bound L being loose. The real gains left are on larger or tighter instances, so the merge is about spending the CPU budget better rather than switching between X and Y.

strategy: PARADIGM: Constraint-propagation makespan descent (schedule-or-postpone CP search). A single code node first validates the instance: unknown job or resource references, demands above capacity, and precedence cycles via Kahn's algorithm. For feasible instances it builds a quick seed schedule and then repeatedly solves the decision problem "is there a schedule with makespan ≤ best−1?". The search is chronological schedule-or-postpone over time windows. At each node, earliest starts are found by timetable propagation against the fixed resource profile. Latest starts come from critical-path tails, and an energetic-reasoning check over [est, lct] windows prunes infeasible nodes. When a job is postponed, its earliest start jumps to the next time another job finishes, and jobs that use no resources are never postponed. The search stops when it proves optimality, reaches the static lower bound, or hits the CPU budget.

A validation node detects unknown references, over-capacity demands and precedence cycles (Kahn's algorithm) and returns "infeasible" for them. The solver computes a strengthened lower bound from the critical path with releases, threshold energy bounds, and disjunctive bounds on greedy cliques of mutually non-overlappable jobs. It seeds a population with several priority rules and randomized variants, each decoded by a serial SGS plus forward-backward improvement. A steady-state Lamarckian GA then evolves activity lists with two-point order crossover, swap and insert mutation, duplicate elimination, and stagnation-triggered re-seeding until the time budget runs out or the lower bound is reached.
change:
DIAGNOSIS: The search space is right, because the serial SGS with forward-backward improvement can reach optimal active schedules. The search over it is weak. Every new candidate is either a fresh noisy priority rule or a random perturbation of the single best schedule's start times. Good partial orderings found in different schedules are never combined, so the search stalls on tightly coupled instances such as the release_times, medium and tight_resources families. The early-stop lower bound is also weak: it ignores jobs that pairwise cannot overlap through precedence or across resources. Time is therefore wasted on instances that are already optimal and missing on hard ones. I replace the random multi-start with a steady-state genetic algorithm over activity lists, in the style of Hartmann's RCPSP GA.
- **Decoding:** each list is decoded by the heap-based serial SGS, so any permutation stays precedence-safe.
- **Improvement and write-back:** each decoded schedule is improved by forward-backward passes. The improved start order is written back into the individual (Lamarckian learning), so offspring inherit the improvement.
- **Operators:** two-point order crossover combines good sub-sequences from two parents. Mutation uses adjacent swaps and insertion moves.
- **Escaping stalls:** a population of distinct schedules is kept, and when progress stalls the worse half is re-seeded from heavy mutations of the best.
- **Lower bound:** I add clique-based disjunctive bounds over a conflict graph (precedence-comparable or resource-incompatible pairs), with release and tail thresholds. I also add threshold-based energy bounds. The search stops early only when the schedule is provably optimal.

strategy: PARADIGM: Iterative Flattening with Precedence-Constraint Posting (a partial-order-schedule search in the style of Cesta, Oddi and Smith). A code node first validates the instance: unknown job or resource references, demand above capacity, and precedence cycles via Kahn's algorithm. For feasible instances, the solver keeps a temporal network of the original precedences plus "posted" precedence edges. It always reads off the earliest-start solution, which is the longest path from the release times. It then repeatedly finds the earliest resource over-subscription and resolves it by posting one ordering between two jobs that overlap there. Two jobs that are both running at a time t can never be ordered either way already, so posting cannot create a cycle. The pair chosen is the one whose posting gives the smallest est(a)+d(a)+tail(b), with randomized noise added. Once flattening has removed all conflicts, the search alternates relaxation (it removes random posted edges, biased towards edges on the critical path) with re-flattening. It accepts non-worsening solutions, resets to the best solution on stagnation, and stops at a computed lower bound or after about 1.15 s. A serial-SGS seed and a left-shift decode of the best schedule act as a safety net, and a final validator checks the result before anything is output.

A prepare node checks feasibility (unknown references, demand above capacity, Kahn cycle detection) and stores preprocessed arrays, bounds and a size flag in state. A GA node with an activity-list encoding, serial SGS and forward-backward justification builds a strong incumbent in about 0.45 s. A branch then routes small instances to a complete branch-and-bound over canonical SGS orders that can prove optimality, followed by a short LNS. Larger instances go straight to a window LNS that exactly re-optimises short segments of the activity list with a tail-bounded DFS while the suffix is re-decoded. A final node validates the schedule and falls back to a sequential schedule if anything fails.
change:
DIAGNOSIS: The GA with serial-SGS and forward-backward improvement already reaches the true optimum on most small and medium instances. For example, two of the weak dev instances are optimal under a disjunctive-clique argument (makespans 40 and 44), so their low scores come from the hidden bound. Real losses remain on larger instances (wide_parallel, long_chains, release_times with 15–40 jobs), and two things cause them. First, the search only moves through global crossover and swap mutations, so it cannot systematically fix the local ordering decisions inside one time slice. Second, the remaining ~0.5 s goes to a full-depth branch-and-bound that cannot finish or improve anything once n is above about 15. That time is effectively wasted on exactly the instances where improvement is still possible. The single monolithic function becomes a graph of five nodes:
- **prepare**: checks feasibility, does the preprocessing and stores it in state.
- **ga_phase**: the existing GA, run as the incumbent builder.
- **branch on instance size**: small instances (≤16 jobs) get the complete branch-and-bound, which can prove optimality, followed by a short LNS. Large instances give their whole remaining budget to the new LNS.
- **lns_phase** (new): a large-neighbourhood search over the activity list. It fixes the prefix, picks a window of 4–7 consecutive jobs, enumerates precedence-feasible orderings of the window with a bounded DFS that prunes on critical-path tails, and re-decodes the fixed suffix by SGS at each leaf. It accepts strict improvements, which are then polished by forward-backward improvement, and takes plateau moves with probability 0.5.
- **finalize**: validates the result and falls back to a sequential schedule if needed.

strategy: PARADIGM: Lagrangian price-coordinated scheduling (dual subgradient over time-indexed resource prices). A validation step detects unknown references, demands above capacity and precedence cycles (Kahn's algorithm), and answers "infeasible" for those. For feasible instances, each resource keeps a price for every time slot. A relaxed problem places each job, in topological order, at the cheapest start inside its precedence and deadline window; prefix sums make each start evaluation O(1). This ignores capacity and pays only the prices. The relaxed starts are turned into a precedence-feasible order, which a serial SGS turns into a valid schedule, followed by forward-backward justification. Prices are then updated by projected subgradient steps on the relaxed overloads, and the deadline is tightened to best-1, until the time budget runs out or the critical-path/energy lower bound is reached.

A single code node first checks feasibility: unknown job or resource references, demand above capacity, and precedence cycles. For feasible instances, a priority-rule and biased-sampling population is decoded by serial SGS with forward-backward justification. A GA with insertion local search then evolves it, followed by a short global branch-and-bound. The new main improvement phase is a large neighbourhood search over windows of the incumbent activity list. Each window is re-sequenced exactly by a small branch-and-bound on top of the fixed prefix profile, and the suffix is re-decoded at each leaf. Window size adapts, equal-makespan sideways moves and restarts from the population add diversity, and every phase stops when the lower bound is reached. A validator with a sequential fallback guarantees a valid output.
change: DIAGNOSIS: Most of the lost score comes from medium and tight instances where the GA plateaus above the optimum. Every GA move is a random edit of an activity list followed by one decode, so the GA never tries all the ways to re-sequence a small group of interacting jobs. The global branch-and-bound has the opposite problem: it is exact, but for 12 or more jobs it cannot finish in its time slice. Nothing in the program combines the two, i.e. searches exactly over a few jobs while keeping the rest of a good schedule fixed. That leaves the remaining time running GA moves that have stopped helping. I add an LNS phase that replaces GA phase 2. It takes the incumbent activity list and picks a contiguous window of k jobs, with k adapting between 4 and 10. It decodes the prefix once onto the resource profile. It then enumerates every precedence-feasible re-ordering of the window with a branch-and-bound that undoes its changes on backtrack. That search uses canonical start-order symmetry breaking, prunes on earliest start plus tail against the incumbent, and re-decodes the fixed suffix at each leaf. When a window yields a better makespan, the result is polished by forward-backward justification and added to the GA population. When the best a window can do is an equal makespan, the search may move sideways to a different schedule with the same makespan to escape plateaus. If it stays stuck, it restarts from members of the population. The existing GA and global branch-and-bound are kept but given shorter time slices to make room for the LNS.

strategy: PARADIGM: Event-time A* over the "chronological decision state" (time t, set of started jobs, running jobs with end times). This is a best-first search over the timeline itself, not over activity lists or SGS orders. One node validates the instance (unknown references, demand above capacity, Kahn cycle detection). The solver gets an upper bound from fast randomized priority-rule SGS sampling. It then runs A* where each node either starts one more eligible, fitting job at the current event time (index-ordered, so each start set is generated once) or advances to the next event (a completion or a release). Zero-duration and resource-free jobs are started eagerly by a provably dominant closure. Identical future states are merged by a canonical key. The admissible heuristic is the maximum of a release- and precedence-aware critical path with tails and a per-resource energy bound. Every candidate schedule is checked by an exact validator before output, and there are fallbacks down to a strictly serial schedule that is always feasible.
